sections.html:
A deed to Massachusetts land is recorded at the registry of deeds for the county or registry district where the land lies. That rule comes from G.L. c. 183, section 4. A conveyance of a fee simple estate is not valid against most outside parties unless it is recorded in the registry for the county or district where the land is.

A few people are bound anyway: the grantor, the grantor's heirs and devisees, and anyone with actual notice of the deed. Still, a buyer should never leave a signed deed in a drawer. Until it is recorded, a later buyer, a creditor or an attachment could win a priority fight against it.

As the seller, you will not usually file the deed yourself. Whoever closes the sale, typically an attorney for the buyer or the buyer's lender, takes it to the right registry after the funds move. You should still know where it goes and how to confirm it landed.

Massachusetts runs two title systems side by side. Deeds to eighty to ninety percent of properties in the Commonwealth are filed as recorded land.

Recorded land works the way most people picture it. The registry stamps each document with a book and page number, and the documents can be viewed online. Registered land is different. Its ownership is described on a Certificate of Title, a decree issued by the Land Court that lists the owner, the land description and any encumbrances.

Registered land is still handled at the county registry, because the Land Court's registered land districts are housed inside the county registries. It does change what you file. Norfolk County, for example, publishes two columns on its fee schedule, one for recorded land and one for the Land Court side, and a document needing both needs two separate checks.

  • Recorded land: indexed by book and page, searchable online.
  • Registered land: tied to a Certificate of Title issued through the Land Court.
  • Not sure which you have: ask your closing attorney or the registry.

sections.h2: What a deed must contain to be accepted
sections.html:
A deed presented for record must carry the grantee's full name, residence and post office address, plus a recital of the full consideration. That is the rule in G.L. c. 183, section 6.

Full consideration means the total price for the conveyance, without deducting any liens or encumbrances the grantee assumes or that remain on the property. If the deed is not given for a set sum of money, it must describe the nature of the other consideration instead. Those endorsements and recitals are recorded as part of the deed.

One detail surprises sellers. Failure to comply does not affect the validity of the deed, yet a register of deeds may not accept a non-compliant deed for recording. A deed can be perfectly good between the parties and still bounce at the counter.

  • Grantee's full legal name and mailing address on the deed or endorsed on it.
  • The stated price in dollars, measured before subtracting a mortgage the buyer takes over.

Recording involves two separate items: a registry recording fee and the deeds excise tax. Each registry sets and posts its own fees, so the safest figure is the one on your registry's current schedule.

As one example, the Norfolk County Registry of Deeds fee schedule lists a deed at $156.00 for recorded land and $155.00 on the Land Court side. A mortgage is $206.00, a mortgage discharge is $106.00 per marginal reference, a declaration of homestead is $36.00 and a municipal lien certificate is $81.00. The registry adds a one dollar postage and document return charge for documents mailed or recorded in person, and as of July 1, 2025 that charge does not apply to electronic filings.

Document or service at NorfolkRecorded landLand Court side
Deed$156.00$155.00
Mortgage$206.00$205.00
Mortgage discharge$106.00$105.00
Declaration of homestead$36.00$35.00
Copies, per page$1.00$1.00

A deed recorded in a different county may cost a different amount. Ask the registry or your attorney for the number that applies.

sections.h2: How the deeds excise tax works
sections.html:
The deeds excise tax is charged on the consideration stated in the deed, per $500 or fraction of $500. The base rate in G.L. c. 64D, section 1 is $2.00 for each additional $500 or fractional part, and in Barnstable County the same section sets $1.50.

The statute applies to deeds where the consideration, not counting liens or encumbrances that remain, exceeds one hundred dollars. It does not apply to an instrument given to secure a debt, or to a deed where the Commonwealth, a city or town, or the United States or their agencies are a party.

The Norfolk County registry collects $2.28 for each $500 and any fraction, and works an example: a $155,000 deed requires $706.80 in excise tax. Pay whatever your registry's current schedule says. It also requires the excise tax to be paid by an attorney's check or a bank check, separate from the recording fee, and no tax is due where consideration is under $100.

  • The tax is computed from the price on the deed, so the stated consideration matters.
  • Who pays the tax is a term of the purchase agreement, so confirm it with your attorney before you sign.
  • A fractional $500 counts as a full $500, so the amount rounds up.

The original signed deed, the recording fee and the excise tax payment, along with whatever else your registry asks for.

Lenders and title insurers usually insist on an attorney, so the closing attorney typically handles all of this. Attorneys are a regular part of buying and selling real estate in Massachusetts, by law and practice. The Supreme Judicial Court's decision in Real Estate Bar Association v. National Real Estate Information Services, 459 Mass. 512 (2011), held that a lender's closing requires an attorney's substantive participation.

  • The signed, acknowledged original deed, not a photocopy.
  • A check or electronic payment for the recording fee, payable as the registry directs.
  • A separate bank or attorney's check for the excise tax.

Norfolk County takes cash or check for recording and copy fees and wants a separate check for each side if a document must be recorded in both the Land Court and the registry.

sections.h2: Checking that your deed was recorded
sections.html:
Search the document on masslandrecords.com or your registry's own site, or sign up for the registry's alert service. Masslandrecords.com is also where you find a copy of your deed and mortgage.

The Secretary of the Commonwealth runs a registry of deeds consumer notification service, which sends an email whenever a new document is recorded against your property. The Norfolk County registry also keeps a page on deed scams for owners.

Your tax assessor is another source. Any Massachusetts owner can look up their deed online along with the property record card the assessors use to generate the tax bill. If a recorded deed does not appear after a few days, call the registry and ask your closing attorney to follow up.

sections.h2: Other state rules that touch a sale
sections.html:
A few rules shape the sale beyond recording. Under G.L. c. 93, section 70, an attorney acting for the mortgagee must render a certification of title to the mortgagor and the mortgagee when a purchase money first mortgage is granted on a dwelling for up to four families that the borrower will occupy.

The state's regulation 760 CMR 74 on residential home inspection waivers also matters. It ensures that sellers of certain residential properties do not condition acceptance of an offer on a waiver of a home inspection and do not accept offers from buyers who have said they intend to waive one. Whether it reaches your sale depends on the property and the buyer, so ask your attorney.

When a house has liens, back taxes or a muddled chain of title, recording is the step where those problems surface. Raise them with your attorney early.

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed in Massachusetts?
faqs.a: At the registry of deeds for the county or registry district where the property lies. G.L. c. 183, section 4 requires recording there for the deed to be valid against most third parties.

faqs.q: How much is the excise tax when I sell my house?
faqs.a: The tax is a set amount per $500 of the price stated in the deed. The Norfolk County registry collects $2.28 per $500 and shows $706.80 on a $155,000 deed, while G.L. c. 64D, section 1 gives a base of $2 per $500. Check your registry for the current rate.

faqs.q: Can a deed be valid but not accepted for recording?
faqs.a: Yes. A missing grantee address or consideration recital does not affect validity under G.L. c. 183, section 6, but a register of deeds may not accept a deed that lacks them.

faqs.q: Does every Massachusetts property use the same title system?
faqs.a: No. Most properties, an estimated eighty to ninety percent, are recorded land, and the rest are registered land with a Certificate of Title through the Land Court.

faqs.q: How do I get a copy of my recorded deed?
faqs.a: Search masslandrecords.com or ask your registry. Norfolk County lists copies at $1.00 per page, plus a postage charge for copies ordered by mail.
